title: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi
tagline: Useful roles of bacteria and fungi in food, medicine, agriculture and industry, and the harmful roles of some bacteria and fungi.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Bacteria and fungi are often thought of only as germs, but most of them are not harmful to people and many are extremely useful. This chapter first separates the general idea of economic importance from the idea of disease, then describes useful roles of bacteria in food making, nitrogen fixation and industry, and useful roles of fungi in food, medicine and in the life of plants and ecosystems. It also discusses harmful bacteria and fungi and the idea of control and prevention, so the topic is balanced rather than negative.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Bacteria and fungi have useful roles as well as harmful ones, and the useful roles are economically important

facts.label: Bacteria
facts.value: Useful in food, nitrogen fixation, medicines and industry; some are harmful

facts.label: Fungi
facts.value: Useful as food, in medicines such as antibiotics, in fermentation and as decomposers; some are harmful

blocks.text: When we talk about the economic importance of an organism, we mean the ways in which it affects human life, work and income. This can be useful or harmful. A bacterium or fungus may be useful because it helps make food or medicine, improves soil, or is used in industry. It may be harmful because it causes disease in people, animals or plants, or spoils food. For bacteria and fungi, the useful roles are often large-scale and planned, while the harmful roles are usually a matter of control and prevention. The important point is that bacteria and fungi are not simply 'good' or 'bad'; they have many different roles.

items.meaning: The ways an organism helps or harms human life, work and resources.
The conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into compounds that plants can use.
Breakdown of food substances by microorganisms, often producing useful products.
A substance produced by some microorganisms that can kill or inhibit other microorganisms.
An organism that feeds on dead and decaying matter and helps recycle nutrients.

items: Economic importance includes both useful and harmful effects.
Bacteria and fungi have many useful roles, not only harmful ones.
Useful roles include food making, fermentation, medicine and soil improvement.
Harmful roles include disease and food spoilage.
Most bacteria and fungi are not harmful to human beings.
Decomposers recycle nutrients and are important in nature.

items.text: Yoghurt and curd are made by the action of bacteria on milk.
items.note: A familiar example of a useful bacterial process in the home.

items.text: Bread, wine and vinegar depend on fermentation by microorganisms.
items.note: Fermentation is one of the oldest uses of microorganisms by people.

blocks.text: Bacteria are useful in several ways. In food, certain bacteria are used to make yoghurt, curd, cheese and other fermented foods. In agriculture, some bacteria, such as Rhizobium, live in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fix atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use, improving the soil. In nature, saprotrophic bacteria break down dead material and help recycle nutrients. In industry and medicine, some bacteria are used to produce antibiotics, enzymes, vitamins and other products. These useful roles show that bacteria are economically important to people, agriculture and ecosystems, not just as germs.

items.meaning: A nitrogen-fixing bacterium that lives in nodules on the roots of leguminous plants.
Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into useful nitrogen compounds for plants.
Bacteria that break down dead and decaying organic matter.
Microbiological breakdown of food substances into useful products.

items: Bacteria are used to make yoghurt, curd and cheese.
Rhizobium fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
Nitrogen fixation improves soil fertility.
Saprotrophic bacteria recycle nutrients by breaking down dead matter.
Some bacteria are used to produce antibiotics and other products.
Bacteria are important in food, agriculture and industry.

items.text: A legume crop such as bean or pea often improves the soil for the next crop because of nitrogen fixation.
items.note: This is one reason crop rotation includes legumes.

items.text: A curd set from warm milk shows bacterial activity in a simple home example.
items.note: The change is caused by bacteria converting lactose and thickening the milk.

blocks.text: Fungi are also economically important in many useful ways. Some fungi are eaten as food, such as mushrooms. Others are used in fermentation to make bread, alcoholic drinks and other products. In medicine, some fungi are the source of antibiotics, such as the original penicillin from a mould. In agriculture and natural ecosystems, saprotrophic fungi break down dead wood, leaves and other organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil. Some fungi live in close association with plant roots and help the plant absorb water and nutrients. So fungi are useful as food, in food making, in medicine, and as decomposers and partners in the soil.

items.meaning: The visible fruiting body of some fungi, used as food.
A substance from a microorganism that can kill or inhibit other microorganisms, such as penicillin from a mould.
Fungi that break down dead organic matter and recycle nutrients.
A close association between two organisms, which may be mutually beneficial.

items: Some fungi are eaten as food, such as mushrooms.
Fungi are used in fermentation to make bread and alcoholic drinks.
Some fungi produce antibiotics used in medicine.
Saprotrophic fungi break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.
Some fungi live in beneficial association with plants.
Fungi are economically important in food, medicine and nature.

items.text: Bread dough rises because of a fungus used in baking, which produces carbon dioxide.
items.note: This is the familiar role of yeast in baking.

items.text: Penicillin was discovered from a mould, showing that fungi can produce useful medicines.
items.note: Antibiotics from fungi are among the most important medical uses of fungi.

blocks.text: Some bacteria and fungi are harmful. Certain bacteria cause diseases in human beings, animals and plants, and some fungi cause diseases too, such as wheat rust and other crop diseases, and some human infections. Some fungi also spoil food, for example by growing on stored grain or fruit. The harmful effects are usually dealt with by prevention, cleanliness, and in the case of disease, by appropriate treatment and protection. In the case of useful microorganisms, it is also important to keep conditions right so that the useful kind grows and the harmful kind does not spoil the product. So control and prevention are important in both protecting health and preserving useful products.

items.meaning: Condition caused by a harmful microorganism or other agent.
Deterioration of food caused by microorganisms or other factors.
Measures to reduce harmful microorganisms or their effects.

items: Some bacteria cause diseases in people, animals and plants.
Some fungi cause crop diseases and human infections.
Some fungi spoil stored food.
Harmful microorganisms are controlled by cleanliness, prevention and treatment.
Useful microorganisms must also be protected from contamination.
The goal is usually control, not complete elimination of all microorganisms.

items.text: Wheat rust is a fungal disease that damages crops and reduces yield.
items.note: A single harmful fungus can affect food supply.

items.text: Spoiled bread or fruit often shows fungal growth, which is why food should be stored properly.
items.note: Food spoilage is one of the everyday harmful roles of fungi.

keyPoints: Economic importance includes useful and harmful effects.
Bacteria are useful in food making, nitrogen fixation, medicine and recycling.

Fungi are useful as food, in fermentation, in antibiotics and as decomposers.

assessment.title: Economic Importance of Bacteria and Fungi: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the organisms and roles clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.prompt: Give two useful roles of bacteria.
exercises.answer: Bacteria are used to make yoghurt and curd from milk, and some bacteria such as Rhizobium fix nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants, improving soil fertility.
exercises.explanation: Any two useful roles, with examples, carry the marks.

exercises.prompt: Give two useful roles of fungi.
exercises.answer: Fungi are used as food, such as mushrooms, and in fermentation, such as yeast in bread and alcoholic drinks. Some fungi produce antibiotics such as penicillin.
exercises.explanation: Any two useful roles, with examples, carry the marks.

exercises.answer: Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds that plants can use.
exercises.explanation: The definition should mention atmospheric nitrogen and plant-usable compounds.

exercises.prompt: Name a bacterium associated with nitrogen fixation.
exercises.answer: Rhizobium, which lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants, is associated with nitrogen fixation.
exercises.explanation: Rhizobium is the standard example of a nitrogen-fixing bacterium in ICSE work.

exercises.prompt: Give one harmful role of fungi and one way to control it.
exercises.answer: Some fungi cause crop diseases such as wheat rust, which reduces yield. This can be controlled by using resistant varieties, good crop management and appropriate treatment.
exercises.explanation: One harmful role and one control measure carry the marks.

exercises.prompt: Why are saprotrophic bacteria and fungi important in nature?
exercises.answer: Saprotrophic bacteria and fungi break down dead and decaying organic matter and return nutrients to the soil, so they recycle materials in nature.
exercises.explanation: The key point is decomposition and nutrient recycling.

questions.prompt: Rhizobium is associated with which process?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium is a nitrogen-fixing bacterium that lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing photosynthesis — bacteria used in food making are different from nitrogen fixers.

questions.prompt: Which is a useful role of fungi?
questions.explanation: Some fungi produce antibiotics such as penicillin.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing only food spoilage — that is one harmful role, not the full picture.

questions.prompt: Yoghurt is made by the action of:
questions.explanation: Yoghurt is made by bacteria acting on milk.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing fungi only — fungi are more closely linked with bread and alcoholic fermentation.

questions.explanation: Saprotrophs break down dead and decaying organic matter and recycle nutrients.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing nitrogen fixation — that is a different useful role, usually by bacteria such as Rhizobium.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a harmful fungal effect?
questions.explanation: Wheat rust is a fungal disease that harms crops.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing bread rising — that is a useful fungal role in baking.

questions.answer: The ways an organism helps or harms human life and resources
questions.explanation: Economic importance includes both useful and harmful effects.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing only harmful effects — that is only part of the idea.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: bacteria that fix nitrogen in legume root nodules are called ________.
questions.explanation: Rhizobium is the nitrogen-fixing bacterium in legume root nodules.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'yeast' — that is a fungus used in fermentation, not a nitrogen fixer.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: one useful fungus product in medicine is an ________, for example penicillin.
questions.explanation: Some fungi produce antibiotics such as penicillin.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'enzyme' — some microorganisms make enzymes, but penicillin is an antibiotic example.

questions.prompt: Give two useful roles of bacteria and one example of each.
questions.answer: Bacteria are used in food making, for example to make yoghurt and curd from milk. They are also useful in agriculture because some bacteria such as Rhizobium fix nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants, improving soil fertility.
questions.explanation: Any two useful roles with examples carry the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Giving roles without examples — examples help show the usefulness.

questions.prompt: Give two useful roles of fungi and one example of each.
questions.answer: Fungi are used as food, for example mushrooms. They are also used in fermentation, such as yeast in bread and alcoholic drinks, and some fungi produce antibiotics such as penicillin.
questions.explanation: Any two useful roles with examples carry the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only food examples and forgetting medicine or fermentation.

questions.prompt: Explain why bacteria and fungi are economically important.
questions.answer: Bacteria and fungi are economically important because they have many useful roles. Bacteria are used to make foods such as yoghurt and curd, and some bacteria such as Rhizobium fix nitrogen in legume root nodules, improving soil fertility. Saprotrophic bacteria break down dead matter and recycle nutrients. Some bacteria are used to produce antibiotics and other products. Fungi are used as food such as mushrooms, in fermentation for bread and alcoholic drinks, and as a source of antibiotics such as penicillin. Saprotrophic fungi also recycle nutrients in nature. In addition to these useful roles, some bacteria and fungi are harmful and cause disease or food spoilage, which is also economically important because it must be prevented or controlled.
questions.explanation: A full answer should cover useful roles of both groups, with examples, and note that harmful roles are also economically important.
questions.commonMistake: Only listing harmful roles and forgetting the useful ones.

questions.prompt: A farmer grows legumes to improve soil before another crop. Which microorganism is most likely to help, and how does it help?
questions.answer: Rhizobium is the microorganism most likely to help. It lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use. This improves the nitrogen supply in the soil, so the next crop can benefit from the improved fertility.
questions.explanation: The answer should name Rhizobium, say that it fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules, and link that to improved soil fertility.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the fungus in the soil helps more than the nitrogen-fixing bacterium — legumes mainly benefit from Rhizobium.
